I'm 47, been farming since I was 22 when my father handed me the reins. Twenty-five years on these fields, and I know every low spot and every sandy patch. I've got 232.9 mu, which is a good chunk of land for Quzhou—bigger than most in the village. With just my wife, my daughter, and me at home, though, we can't do it alone. I hire workers for the busy seasons and rent machinery for planting and harvest. You have to, at this scale.

My main system is wheat-maize double crop on 200 mu. That's the backbone—reliable buyers, I know the routine, and the machinery's set up for it. The other 32.9 mu I'm putting in cauliflower come March. It's more work and more risk, but the price can be good, and I've got a standing buyer at the county market. Last year the cauliflower paid off, so I'm sticking with it.

For the wheat, I'm planting in mid-October like always. I'm using Jinmai 47, an improved variety. Costs about 25 yuan per mu for seed. For fertilizer, the extension agent keeps saying 18 kg nitrogen per mu is enough, but I've tried that and I ended up at 480 kg/mu last year. I want 500 kg/mu, so I'm going with 20 kg N per mu. I put down compound fertilizer at planting—about 50 kg per mu—then topdress urea at jointing, about 25 kg per mu. That gives me my 20 kg N plus some P and K. I'll irrigate four times: planting, overwintering, jointing, and grain-filling. Water isn't cheap anymore with the meters, but you can't skip it if you want good yield. For pests, I'll spray herbicide once in spring and watch for rust—I might do a fungicide if it looks bad.

The maize goes in right after wheat harvest in early June. That's the hard part—sometimes I've got five days, sometimes less. I use no-till planting when the stubble isn't too thick; saves time and money. Zhengdan 958 hybrid, about 30 yuan per mu for seed. Fertilizer is similar: compound at planting, urea at big trumpet stage. Around 18 kg N per mu total. Two irrigations usually, three if July is dry. Targeting 550 kg/mu if the weather cooperates.

Cauliflower is different. I start seedlings in February, transplant in March. It's labor-heavy—transplanting, hilling, tying leaves. I hire 8 to 10 workers for the peak times. I put down chicken manure as base, then compound fertilizer, then topdress with urea when the heads start forming. Heavy feeder, so I go heavier on fertilizer—about 25 kg N per mu. Irrigate every week or two, six times total. Yield should be around 1,200 kg per mu if the heads form well. Pesticide is heavier too—diamondback moth is always a problem.

Total costs this year will run about 165,000 yuan. That's a big outlay, but at this scale you have to spend to earn. My daughter's school fees are coming up, and I need to set aside cash for the harvest labor. I'd rather put down a bit more fertilizer than risk a bad year. That's how I've stayed in business this long.
